reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: The most common porphyria overall and the prototypical cutaneous, non-acute porphyria caused by reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity
Presents with skin fragility and blistering on sun-exposed areas, especially the backs of the hands, forearms and face
Skin lesions include vesicles and bullae, erosions, milia, scarring, hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis
Most cases are acquired (type 1); a minority are familial (type 2) with inherited enzyme deficiency, and iron overload is a central contributor in both
Strongly associated with hepatitis C infection, alcohol excess, oestrogen use, HIV, and haemochromatosis gene mutations, all of which promote hepatic iron loading
Diagnosis is supported by raised urinary uroporphyrins with a characteristic porphyrin pattern and often pink-red urine fluorescing under Wood's light

Management principles include removing precipitants (alcohol, oestrogens), treating underlying hepatitis C, and reducing iron burden by phlebotomy, with low-dose antimalarials as an alternative therapy
Unlike the acute hepatic porphyrias, PCT does not cause neurovisceral attacks
Screening for hepatitis C, HIV, and hereditary haemochromatosis is warranted at diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Porphyria cutanea tarda results from deficient activity of hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), the fifth enzyme of haem biosynthesis. Reduced enzyme activity leads to accumulation and hepatic overproduction of highly carboxylated porphyrinogens, which are oxidised to porphyrins that deposit in the skin. On light exposure these porphyrins generate reactive oxygen species that damage the dermo-epidermal junction, producing the characteristic photosensitive blistering. Hepatic iron and oxidative stress inhibit UROD activity, which is why iron overload, alcohol, oestrogens, hepatitis C and HIV are strong susceptibility factors; the disorder may be sporadic (acquired) or familial with an inherited partial enzyme deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria (which can also cause skin fragility)
Bullous pemphigoid and other autoimmune blistering diseases
additionalInvestigations: Urinary porphyrin profile showing predominant uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin
Plasma porphyrin fluorescence scan and faecal porphyrin analysis to distinguish from variegate porphyria
Iron studies including ferritin and transferrin saturation
Hepatitis C, HIV and liver function testing
HFE genotyping for hereditary haemochromatosis when iron overload is present
redFlags: Underlying chronic liver disease with progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma
Unrecognised hepatitis C or HIV coinfection
Significant iron overload with end-organ effects
Extensive skin ulceration with secondary infection
reference.prognosis: PCT generally responds well to removal of precipitants, treatment of hepatitis C, and iron depletion, with clinical and biochemical remission achievable in most patients. Long-term outlook is largely determined by any associated liver disease, with a risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in those with chronic hepatitis or continued alcohol use.
pitfalls: Failing to search for and treat hepatitis C or other liver disease
Overlooking iron overload as the key modifiable driver
Continuing oestrogens or alcohol that perpetuate the condition
Confusing PCT with the acute hepatic porphyrias and mismanaging accordingly
Missing coexisting variegate porphyria, which can also blister but carries acute attack risk
